lessons.title: Complex Conditions
lessons.content: Combine multiple conditions in WHERE using AND, OR, and parentheses. Example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Total > 100 AND (Status = 'Shipped' OR Status = 'Delivered');

lessons.question: What do parentheses do in a WHERE clause?

lessons.title: Using IN
lessons.content: IN checks if a value is in a list. Example: SELECT Name FROM Customers WHERE City IN ('Paris', 'London');

lessons.question: What does WHERE City IN ('Paris', 'London') do?

lessons.title: Using BETWEEN
lessons.content: BETWEEN selects a range, inclusive. Example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE OrderDate BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-12-31';

lessons.question: What does BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-12-31' select?

lessons.title: Combining Operators
lessons.content: Combine IN, BETWEEN, and comparisons. Example: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE Price BETWEEN 10 AND 50 AND Category IN ('Electronics', 'Clothing');

lessons.question: Can you combine BETWEEN and IN in WHERE?

lessons.title: Nested Conditions
lessons.content: Use nested conditions for complex logic. Example: SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE (Salary > 50000 OR Department = 'IT') AND HireDate > '2020-01-01';

lessons.question: What does (Salary > 50000 OR Department = 'IT') AND HireDate > '2020-01-01' require?
options: Salary or Department true, plus HireDate
lessons.correct: Salary or Department true, plus HireDate

lessons.title: Precedence in WHERE
lessons.content: AND is evaluated before OR. Use parentheses to control order. Example: WHERE A OR B AND C means WHERE A OR (B AND C).

lessons.question: Which operator is evaluated first in WHERE?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Complex WHERE clauses can slow queries. Ensure indexes exist on filtered columns like Price or OrderDate.

lessons.question: What improves WHERE clause performance?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL for NULL checks. Example: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE City IS NULL;

lessons.title: The LIKE Operator
lessons.content: LIKE matches patterns in text. Example: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Name LIKE 'A%'; gets names starting with A.

lessons.question: What does LIKE 'A%' match?

lessons.title: Wildcard %
lessons.content: The % wildcard matches any characters. Example: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE Name LIKE '%phone%'; finds names containing 'phone'.

lessons.question: What does '%phone%' match?

lessons.title: Wildcard _
lessons.content: The _ wildcard matches one character. Example: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Name LIKE 'J_n'; matches Jon, Jan, etc.

lessons.question: What does 'J_n' match?

lessons.title: Combining Wildcards
lessons.content: Use % and _ together. Example: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE Code LIKE 'A_1%'; matches A11, A21, etc.

lessons.question: What does 'A_1%' match?

lessons.title: NOT LIKE
lessons.content: NOT LIKE excludes patterns. Example: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Name NOT LIKE 'B%'; excludes names starting with B.

lessons.question: What does NOT LIKE 'B%' do?

lessons.title: Case Sensitivity
lessons.content: LIKE may be case-sensitive depending on the database. Use LOWER() for consistency. Example: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE LOWER(Name) LIKE 'a%';

lessons.question: How do you handle case sensitivity with LIKE?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: LIKE with leading % (e.g., '%phone') prevents index use, slowing queries. Avoid if possible.

lessons.question: Why avoid LIKE with leading %?

lessons.title: Combining with Other Conditions
lessons.content: Use LIKE with AND/OR. Example: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE Name LIKE '%phone%' AND Price > 500;

modules.title: Working with IN and NOT IN

lessons.title: The IN Operator
lessons.content: IN matches a value against a list. Example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Status IN ('Pending', 'Shipped');

lessons.question: What does IN ('Pending', 'Shipped') do?

lessons.title: NOT IN Operator
lessons.content: NOT IN excludes values in a list. Example: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Country NOT IN ('USA', 'UK');

lessons.question: What does NOT IN ('USA', 'UK') do?

lessons.title: IN with Subqueries
lessons.content: Use IN with subqueries. Example: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE Category IN (SELECT Category FROM Categories WHERE Active = 1);

lessons.question: Can IN be used with a subquery?

lessons.title: Empty Lists
lessons.content: An empty IN list returns no rows. Example: SELECT * FROM Pets WHERE Type IN (); returns nothing.

lessons.question: What does IN () return?

lessons.title: Combining with Other Conditions
lessons.content: Use IN with AND/OR. Example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerID IN (1, 2, 3) AND Total > 100;

lessons.question: Can IN be combined with AND?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: IN with large lists or subqueries can be slow. Consider JOIN for better performance with subqueries.

lessons.question: What can be faster than IN with a subquery?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: IN does not match NULL values. Use IS NULL separately. Example: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE City IN ('Paris', NULL); won’t match NULLs.

lessons.question: Does IN match NULL values?

lessons.title: Text and Numbers
lessons.content: IN works with text and numbers. Example: SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE DepartmentID IN (101, 102);

lessons.title: The BETWEEN Operator
lessons.content: BETWEEN selects values in a range, inclusive. Example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Total BETWEEN 100 AND 500;

lessons.question: Is BETWEEN inclusive of its endpoints?

lessons.title: Using with Dates
lessons.content: BETWEEN works with dates. Example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE OrderDate BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-12-31';

lessons.question: Can BETWEEN be used with dates?

lessons.title: NOT BETWEEN
lessons.content: NOT BETWEEN excludes a range. Example: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE Price NOT BETWEEN 10 AND 50;

lessons.question: What does NOT BETWEEN 10 AND 50 do?

lessons.title: Combining with Other Conditions
lessons.content: Use BETWEEN with AND/OR. Example: SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE Salary BETWEEN 40000 AND 60000 AND Department = 'Sales';

lessons.question: Can BETWEEN be combined with AND?

lessons.title: Numbers vs. Text
lessons.content: BETWEEN works with numbers and text. Example: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Name BETWEEN 'A' AND 'M'; gets names from A to M.

lessons.question: Can BETWEEN be used with text?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: BETWEEN uses indexes effectively if columns like Price or OrderDate are indexed.

lessons.question: Does BETWEEN benefit from indexes?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: BETWEEN does not match NULL values. Use IS NULL separately to handle NULLs.

lessons.question: Does BETWEEN match NULL values?

lessons.title: Edge Cases
lessons.content: Ensure the lower bound is less than the upper bound. Example: BETWEEN 100 AND 50 is invalid.

lessons.title: Multiple Joins
lessons.content: Join multiple tables. Example: SELECT c.Name, o.OrderDate, p.Name FROM Customers c INNER JOIN Orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID INNER JOIN Products p ON o.ProductID = p.ProductID;

lessons.question: What does joining multiple tables do?

lessons.title: Self Joins
lessons.content: Join a table to itself. Example: SELECT e1.Name, e2.Name AS Manager FROM Employees e1 INNER JOIN Employees e2 ON e1.ManagerID = e2.EmployeeID;

lessons.question: What is a self join?

lessons.title: Non-Equi Joins
lessons.content: Use operators like > or <. Example: SELECT * FROM Products p1 INNER JOIN Products p2 ON p1.Price > p2.Price;

lessons.question: What operator can be used in a non-equi join?

lessons.title: Join with WHERE
lessons.content: Combine JOIN with WHERE. Example: SELECT c.Name FROM Customers c INNER JOIN Orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID WHERE o.Total > 100;

lessons.question: Can WHERE be used with JOIN?

lessons.title: Join Order
lessons.content: Join order can affect performance. Place smaller tables first and ensure indexes on join columns.

lessons.question: What can improve JOIN performance?

lessons.title: Ambiguous Columns
lessons.content: Use table aliases to avoid ambiguity. Example: SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name FROM Customers c INNER JOIN Orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID;

lessons.question: How do you avoid ambiguous column names in joins?

lessons.title: Complex Join Conditions
lessons.content: Use multiple conditions in ON. Example: SELECT * FROM Orders o INNER JOIN Customers c ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID AND c.City = 'London';

lessons.question: Can ON include multiple conditions?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Multiple joins increase query complexity. Optimize with indexes and limit result sets.

lessons.title: What Are Outer Joins?
lessons.content: Outer joins include unmatched rows from one or both tables. Types: LEFT, RIGHT, FULL. Example: SELECT c.Name, o.OrderID FROM Customers c LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID;

lessons.question: What does an outer join include?

lessons.title: LEFT JOIN
lessons.content: LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table. Example: SELECT c.Name, o.Total FROM Customers c LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID; includes customers without orders.

lessons.question: What does LEFT JOIN keep?

lessons.title: RIGHT JOIN
lessons.content: RIGHT JOIN keeps all rows from the right table. Example: SELECT c.Name, o.Total FROM Customers c RIGHT JOIN Orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID; includes orders without customers.

lessons.question: What does RIGHT JOIN keep?

lessons.title: FULL JOIN
lessons.content: FULL JOIN keeps all rows from both tables. Example: SELECT c.Name, o.OrderID FROM Customers c FULL JOIN Orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID; includes all customers and orders.

lessons.question: What does FULL JOIN include?

lessons.title: Handling NULLs
lessons.content: Outer joins produce NULLs for unmatched rows. Example: In a LEFT JOIN, Orders columns are NULL for customers without orders.

lessons.question: What appears in unmatched rows of an outer join?

lessons.title: Filtering with Outer Joins
lessons.content: Use WHERE carefully with outer joins to avoid losing unmatched rows. Example: SELECT c.Name FROM Customers c LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID WHERE o.OrderID IS NULL; finds customers with no orders.

lessons.question: What can WHERE o.OrderID IS NULL find in a LEFT JOIN?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Outer joins can be slower than INNER JOINs. Ensure indexes on join columns and limit result sets.

lessons.question: What improves outer join performance?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Outer joins are useful for reporting, like finding all customers, including those without orders, or all products, including those not sold.

lessons.title: What is a Cross Join?
lessons.content: CROSS JOIN combines every row from two tables. Example: SELECT * FROM Colors CROSS JOIN Sizes; pairs every color with every size.

lessons.question: What does a CROSS JOIN produce?

lessons.title: Syntax
lessons.content: Use CROSS JOIN or a comma. Example: SELECT c.Name, s.Size FROM Colors c CROSS JOIN Sizes s; or SELECT c.Name, s.Size FROM Colors c, Sizes s;

lessons.question: Which is a valid CROSS JOIN syntax?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: CROSS JOIN is useful for generating combinations, like all possible product variations (e.g., color-size pairs).

lessons.question: What is a common use for CROSS JOIN?

lessons.title: Result Size
lessons.content: If table A has 10 rows and table B has 5, CROSS JOIN yields 50 rows (10 × 5). Be cautious with large tables.

lessons.question: How many rows from a CROSS JOIN of 3-row and 4-row tables?

lessons.title: Filtering Cross Joins
lessons.content: Use WHERE to filter results. Example: SELECT c.Name, s.Size FROM Colors c CROSS JOIN Sizes s WHERE s.Size = 'Large';

lessons.question: Can WHERE be used with CROSS JOIN?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: CROSS JOINs can produce large result sets. Limit rows with WHERE or use smaller tables.

lessons.question: Why be cautious with CROSS JOIN?

lessons.title: Avoiding Accidental Cross Joins
lessons.content: Omitting ON in a JOIN can cause a CROSS JOIN. Always specify join conditions for INNER or OUTER joins.

lessons.question: What causes an accidental CROSS JOIN?

lessons.title: Practical Example
lessons.content: CROSS JOIN can generate test data. Example: SELECT e.Name, d.Date FROM Employees e CROSS JOIN Dates d; creates all employee-date combinations.

lessons.title: What is a Self Join?
lessons.content: A self join joins a table to itself. Example: SELECT e1.Name, e2.Name AS Manager FROM Employees e1 INNER JOIN Employees e2 ON e1.ManagerID = e2.EmployeeID;

lessons.question: What does a self join do?

lessons.title: Hierarchical Data
lessons.content: Self joins are ideal for hierarchical data like employee-manager relationships or category-subcategory structures.

lessons.question: What is a common use for self joins?

lessons.title: Using Aliases
lessons.content: Aliases are required to distinguish table instances. Example: e1 and e2 in SELECT e1.Name, e2.Name FROM Employees e1 JOIN Employees e2;

lessons.question: Are aliases required in self joins?

lessons.title: LEFT Self Join
lessons.content: Use LEFT JOIN to include top-level rows. Example: SELECT e1.Name, e2.Name AS Manager FROM Employees e1 LEFT JOIN Employees e2 ON e1.ManagerID = e2.EmployeeID; includes employees without managers.

lessons.question: What does a LEFT self join include?

lessons.title: Multiple Self Joins
lessons.content: Join the table multiple times for deeper hierarchies, like grandparent-parent-child relationships.

lessons.question: Can a table be self-joined multiple times?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Ensure indexes on columns used in self joins (e.g., ManagerID) to improve query speed.

lessons.question: What improves self join performance?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: In a LEFT self join, NULL appears for rows without matches (e.g., top-level employees with no manager).

lessons.question: What appears for unmatched rows in a LEFT self join?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Self joins are used for organizational charts, bill of materials, or category trees in databases.

lessons.title: What is a Subquery?
lessons.content: A subquery is a query nested inside another query. Example: SELECT Name FROM Customers WHERE CustomerID IN (SELECT CustomerID FROM Orders WHERE Total > 1000);

lessons.question: What is a subquery?

lessons.title: Subqueries in WHERE
lessons.content: Use subqueries in WHERE to filter rows. Example: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE Price > (SELECT AVG(Price) FROM Products);

lessons.question: Where can subqueries be used?

lessons.title: Subqueries in SELECT
lessons.content: Use subqueries in SELECT for per-row calculations. Example: SELECT Name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID) AS OrderCount FROM Customers c;

lessons.question: Can subqueries be used in SELECT?

lessons.title: Subqueries in FROM
lessons.content: Use subqueries in FROM as derived tables. Example: SELECT * FROM (SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) AS Orders FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID) AS Sub WHERE Orders > 5;

lessons.question: What is a subquery in FROM called?

lessons.title: Single vs. Multi-Row
lessons.content: Single-row subqueries return one row (use =, >). Multi-row subqueries return multiple rows (use IN, ANY, ALL).

lessons.question: What operator is used with multi-row subqueries?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Subqueries can be slower than JOINs. Rewrite as JOIN where possible for better performance.

lessons.question: What can be faster than a subquery?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: Subqueries returning NULL can affect results. Example: WHERE x IN (SELECT y WHERE y IS NULL) may return no rows.

lessons.question: What happens if a subquery returns NULL with IN?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Subqueries are useful for filtering based on aggregates or finding rows matching conditions in another table.

lessons.title: What is a Correlated Subquery?
lessons.content: A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query, running for each row. Example: SELECT Name FROM Customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Orders o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID);

lessons.question: What makes a subquery correlated?

lessons.title: Using EXISTS
lessons.content: EXISTS checks if a subquery returns rows. Example: SELECT * FROM Products p WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Orders o WHERE o.ProductID = p.ProductID);

lessons.question: What does EXISTS check?

lessons.title: NOT EXISTS
lessons.content: NOT EXISTS checks for no rows. Example: SELECT * FROM Customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Orders o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID);

lessons.question: What does NOT EXISTS find?

lessons.title: Correlated in SELECT
lessons.content: Use in SELECT for per-row calculations. Example: SELECT Name, (SELECT SUM(Total) FROM Orders o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID) AS TotalSpent FROM Customers c;

lessons.question: Can correlated subqueries be in SELECT?

lessons.title: Performance Impact
lessons.content: Correlated subqueries run per row, so they can be slow. Consider JOIN or CTEs for optimization.

lessons.question: Why are correlated subqueries slow?

lessons.title: Comparison Operators
lessons.content: Use >, =, etc. Example: SELECT * FROM Products p WHERE Price > (SELECT AVG(Price) FROM Products p2 WHERE p2.Category = p.Category);

lessons.question: Can correlated subqueries use >?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: Correlated subqueries with NULLs can lead to unexpected results. Test carefully with IS NULL.

lessons.question: What should you test for with correlated subqueries?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Correlated subqueries are useful for row-by-row comparisons, like finding products above their category’s average price.

lessons.title: What is a CTE?
lessons.content: A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a temporary result set defined with WITH. Example: WITH TopOrders AS (SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Total > 1000) SELECT * FROM TopOrders;

lessons.question: What is a CTE?

lessons.title: CTE Syntax
lessons.content: Use WITH followed by a name and query. Example: WITH Sales AS (SELECT CustomerID, SUM(Total) AS Total FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID) SELECT * FROM Sales WHERE Total > 5000;

lessons.question: What keyword starts a CTE?

lessons.title: Multiple CTEs
lessons.content: Define multiple CTEs with commas. Example: WITH A AS (SELECT * FROM Orders), B AS (SELECT * FROM A WHERE Total > 100) SELECT * FROM B;

lessons.question: Can you define multiple CTEs?

lessons.title: CTEs vs. Subqueries
lessons.content: CTEs are more readable than nested subqueries and can be reused in a query. They often perform similarly to subqueries.

lessons.question: What is an advantage of CTEs?

lessons.title: Recursive CTEs
lessons.content: Recursive CTEs handle hierarchical data. Example: WITH RECURSIVE Tree AS (...) for traversing employee-manager hierarchies.

lessons.question: What can recursive CTEs handle?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: CTEs are not materialized in some databases (e.g., MySQL). Avoid complex logic in CTEs for better performance.

lessons.question: Are CTEs always materialized?

lessons.title: Joining CTEs
lessons.content: Join CTEs like tables. Example: WITH Sales AS (SELECT CustomerID, SUM(Total) AS Total FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID) SELECT c.Name, s.Total FROM Customers c JOIN Sales s ON c.CustomerID = s.CustomerID;

lessons.question: Can CTEs be joined like tables?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: CTEs simplify complex queries, improve readability, and are ideal for hierarchical or multi-step calculations.

lessons.title: What Are Window Functions?
lessons.content: Window functions perform calculations across rows without grouping. Example: SELECT Name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY Price) AS RowNum FROM Products;

lessons.question: What do window functions avoid?

lessons.title: ROW_NUMBER()
lessons.content: Assigns a unique number to each row. Example: SELECT Name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Category ORDER BY Price) AS Rank FROM Products;

lessons.question: What does ROW_NUMBER() assign?

lessons.title: PARTITION BY
lessons.content: Divides rows into groups. Example: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Category ORDER BY Price) resets numbering per category.

lessons.question: What does PARTITION BY do?

lessons.title: RANK()
lessons.content: Assigns ranks, with ties getting the same rank. Example: SELECT Name, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Price DESC) AS Rank FROM Products;

lessons.question: How does RANK() handle ties?

lessons.title: DENSE_RANK()
lessons.content: Like RANK(), but no gaps in ranking. Example: SELECT Name, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Price DESC) AS Rank FROM Products;

lessons.question: What is unique about DENSE_RANK()?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Window functions require sorting, so use indexes on ORDER BY columns (e.g., Price) for efficiency.

lessons.question: What improves window function performance?

lessons.title: OVER Clause
lessons.content: The OVER clause defines the window. Example: OVER (PARTITION BY Category ORDER BY Price) sets the scope for ROW_NUMBER().

lessons.question: What defines the scope of a window function?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Window functions are used for ranking, numbering, or calculating metrics like top products per category.

lessons.title: Aggregate Window Functions
lessons.content: Use SUM(), AVG(), etc., over a window. Example: SELECT Name, Price, SUM(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category) AS CategoryTotal FROM Products;

lessons.question: What can SUM() do in a window function?

lessons.title: Running Totals
lessons.content: Calculate running totals with ORDER BY. Example: SELECT OrderID, Total, SUM(Total) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate) AS RunningTotal FROM Orders;

lessons.question: What does ORDER BY in SUM() OVER create?

lessons.title: AVG() Over Window
lessons.content: Compute averages per partition. Example: SELECT Name, Price, AVG(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category) AS AvgPrice FROM Products;

lessons.question: What does AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY Category) compute?

lessons.title: COUNT() Over Window
lessons.content: Count rows in a window. Example: SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID) AS OrderCount FROM Orders;

lessons.question: What does COUNT(*) OVER compute?

lessons.title: Combining Aggregates
lessons.content: Use multiple window functions. Example: SELECT Name, Price, SUM(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category), AVG(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category) FROM Products;

lessons.question: Can multiple window functions be used in one query?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Aggregate window functions can be costly. Use indexes on PARTITION BY and ORDER BY columns.

lessons.question: What improves aggregate window function performance?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: Aggregate window functions ignore NULLs in calculations, similar to regular aggregates.

lessons.question: Do aggregate window functions include NULLs in calculations?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Aggregate window functions are used for running totals, category averages, or counting occurrences without grouping.

lessons.title: LAG() Function
lessons.content: LAG() accesses the previous row’s value. Example: SELECT OrderID, Total, LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate) AS PrevTotal FROM Orders;

lessons.question: What does LAG() access?

lessons.title: LEAD() Function
lessons.content: LEAD() accesses the next row’s value. Example: SELECT OrderID, Total, LEAD(Total) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate) AS NextTotal FROM Orders;

lessons.question: What does LEAD() access?

lessons.title: Frame Specification
lessons.content: Define a window frame with ROWS or RANGE. Example: SUM(Total) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW);

lessons.question: What does ROWS BETWEEN define?

lessons.title: NTILE()
lessons.content: NTILE(n) divides rows into n buckets. Example: SELECT Name, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY Price) AS Quartile FROM Products;

lessons.question: What does NTILE(4) create?

lessons.title: FIRST_VALUE()
lessons.content: Returns the first value in a window. Example: SELECT Name, FIRST_VALUE(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category ORDER BY Price) AS MinPrice FROM Products;

lessons.question: What does FIRST_VALUE() return?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Advanced window functions like LAG() require sorting. Index ORDER BY columns for better performance.

lessons.question: What improves LAG() performance?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: LAG() and LEAD() return NULL for missing rows (e.g., first or last row in a partition).

lessons.question: What do LAG() and LEAD() return for missing rows?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Advanced window functions are used for time-series analysis, like comparing sales to previous periods.

lessons.title: What is GROUPING SETS?
lessons.content: GROUPING SETS allows multiple grouping levels in one query. Example: SELECT Category, Region, SUM(Sales) FROM Orders GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (Category, Region);

lessons.question: What does GROUPING SETS do?

lessons.title: CUBE
lessons.content: CUBE generates all possible combinations of groups. Example: SELECT Category, Region, SUM(Sales) FROM Orders GROUP BY CUBE (Category, Region);

lessons.question: What does CUBE generate?

lessons.title: ROLLUP
lessons.content: ROLLUP creates hierarchical subtotals. Example: SELECT Category, Region, SUM(Sales) FROM Orders GROUP BY ROLLUP (Category, Region);

lessons.question: What does ROLLUP create?

lessons.title: GROUPING Function
lessons.content: GROUPING(column) identifies summary rows. Returns 1 for aggregated rows. Example: SELECT Category, GROUPING(Category) FROM Orders GROUP BY CUBE (Category);

lessons.question: What does GROUPING(Category) return for summary rows?

lessons.title: Combining with Aggregates
lessons.content: Use with SUM(), COUNT(), etc. Example: SELECT Category, Region, COUNT(*) FROM Orders GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (Category, (Category, Region));

lessons.question: Can GROUPING SETS use COUNT()?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: CUBE and ROLLUP can generate many rows. Use GROUPING SETS for specific combinations to improve efficiency.

lessons.question: What is more efficient than CUBE?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: Summary rows in CUBE/ROLLUP may show NULL for non-aggregated columns. Use GROUPING() to distinguish.

lessons.question: How do you distinguish summary rows in CUBE?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: GROUPING SETS and CUBE are used for multi-level reporting, like sales summaries by category and region.

lessons.title: What is Pivoting?
lessons.content: Pivoting converts rows to columns for reporting. Example: SELECT * FROM (SELECT Category, Month, Sales FROM Orders) PIVOT (SUM(Sales) FOR Month IN ('Jan', 'Feb')); (syntax varies by DBMS).

lessons.question: What does pivoting do?

lessons.title: Conditional Aggregation
lessons.content: Without PIVOT, use CASE. Example: SELECT Category, SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Jan' THEN Sales END) AS Jan FROM Orders GROUP BY Category;

lessons.question: What can replace PIVOT in some databases?

lessons.title: PIVOT Syntax
lessons.content: PIVOT requires a source query, aggregate, and column values. Example: PIVOT (SUM(Sales) FOR Month IN ('Jan', 'Feb'));

lessons.question: What does PIVOT require?

lessons.title: Unpivoting
lessons.content: UNPIVOT converts columns to rows. Example: SELECT * FROM SalesTable UNPIVOT (Sales FOR Month IN (Jan, Feb)); (syntax varies by DBMS).

lessons.question: What does UNPIVOT do?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Pivoting can be resource-intensive. Use indexes on grouping columns and limit data before pivoting.

lessons.question: What improves pivoting performance?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: PIVOT may produce NULLs for missing data. Use COALESCE to handle them. Example: COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Jan' THEN Sales END), 0).

lessons.question: How do you handle NULLs in pivoting?

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: PIVOT/UNPIVOT is supported in SQL Server, Oracle; others use CASE. Check your DBMS documentation.

lessons.question: Which DBMS might not support PIVOT?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Pivoting is used for reports like sales by month or category, creating spreadsheet-like outputs.

lessons.title: Advanced GROUP BY
lessons.content: Use GROUP BY with multiple columns. Example: SELECT Category, Region, SUM(Sales) FROM Orders GROUP BY Category, Region;

lessons.question: What does GROUP BY with Category, Region do?

lessons.title: HAVING Clause
lessons.content: Filter groups with HAVING. Example: SELECT Category, SUM(Sales) FROM Orders GROUP BY Category HAVING SUM(Sales) > 10000;

lessons.question: What does HAVING filter?

lessons.title: Filtered Aggregates
lessons.content: Use FILTER (in some DBMS) or CASE. Example: SELECT Category, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE Status = 'Shipped') AS Shipped FROM Orders GROUP BY Category;

lessons.question: What does FILTER in COUNT(*) do?

lessons.title: Multiple Aggregates
lessons.content: Combine aggregates. Example: SELECT Category, SUM(Sales), AVG(Sales) FROM Orders GROUP BY Category;

lessons.question: Can you combine SUM() and AVG() in one query?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: Aggregates like SUM() and AVG() ignore NULLs. Example: SUM(Sales) skips NULL Sales values.

lessons.question: Do aggregates include NULLs?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Use indexes on GROUP BY and HAVING columns to improve aggregation performance.

lessons.question: What improves aggregation performance?

lessons.title: Distinct Aggregates
lessons.content: Use DISTINCT in aggregates. Example: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) FROM Orders;

lessons.question: What does COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) do?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Advanced aggregations are used for summary reports, like total sales by region or filtered order counts.

lessons.title: What is a Stored Procedure?
lessons.content: A stored procedure is a precompiled SQL routine stored in the database. Example: CREATE PROCEDURE GetHighOrders AS SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Total > 1000;

lessons.question: What is a stored procedure?

lessons.title: Creating Procedures
lessons.content: Use CREATE PROCEDURE. Example: CREATE PROCEDURE GetOrders AS SELECT * FROM Orders; (syntax varies by DBMS).

lessons.question: What keyword creates a stored procedure?

lessons.title: Executing Procedures
lessons.content: Call procedures with CALL or EXEC. Example: CALL GetOrders; or EXEC GetOrders;

lessons.question: How do you execute a stored procedure?

lessons.title: Benefits
lessons.content: Stored procedures improve performance, security, and maintainability by encapsulating logic.

lessons.question: What is a benefit of stored procedures?

lessons.title: Modifying Procedures
lessons.content: Use ALTER PROCEDURE to modify. Example: ALTER PROCEDURE GetOrders AS SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Total > 500; (syntax varies).

lessons.question: How do you modify a stored procedure?

lessons.title: Dropping Procedures
lessons.content: Use DROP PROCEDURE to remove. Example: DROP PROCEDURE GetOrders;

lessons.question: What removes a stored procedure?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Stored procedures are precompiled, reducing execution time compared to ad-hoc queries.

lessons.question: Why are stored procedures faster?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Stored procedures are used for repetitive tasks, like generating reports or updating data.

lessons.title: Parameterized Procedures
lessons.content: Stored procedures can accept parameters. Example: CREATE PROCEDURE GetOrdersByStatus (IN status VARCHAR(50)) AS SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Status = status;

lessons.question: What can stored procedures accept?

lessons.title: Input Parameters
lessons.content: Use IN for input. Example: CREATE PROCEDURE GetOrdersByCustomer (IN custID INT) AS SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerID = custID;

lessons.question: What does IN specify in a procedure?

lessons.title: Output Parameters
lessons.content: Use OUT to return values. Example: CREATE PROCEDURE GetOrderCount (IN custID INT, OUT count INT) AS SELECT COUNT(*) INTO count FROM Orders WHERE CustomerID = custID;

lessons.question: What does OUT do in a procedure?

lessons.title: Calling with Parameters
lessons.content: Pass parameters when calling. Example: CALL GetOrdersByStatus('Shipped'); or EXEC GetOrdersByCustomer(101);

lessons.question: How do you pass a parameter to a procedure?

lessons.title: Multiple Parameters
lessons.content: Use multiple parameters. Example: CREATE PROCEDURE GetOrdersByRange (IN minTotal DECIMAL, IN maxTotal DECIMAL) AS SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Total BETWEEN minTotal AND maxTotal;

lessons.question: Can procedures have multiple parameters?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Parameterized procedures prevent SQL injection and improve execution plans.

lessons.question: What prevents SQL injection in procedures?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: Handle NULL parameters carefully. Example: Use COALESCE to set defaults in the procedure.

lessons.question: How do you handle NULL parameters?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Parameterized procedures are used for dynamic filtering, like orders by customer or date range.

lessons.title: What is a Trigger?
lessons.content: A trigger is an automatic action executed on data changes. Example: CREATE TRIGGER LogInsert AFTER INSERT ON Orders FOR EACH ROW INSERT INTO AuditLog (Action) VALUES ('Insert');

lessons.question: What is a trigger?

lessons.title: Trigger Types
lessons.content: Triggers can be BEFORE or AFTER for INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. Example: BEFORE INSERT to validate data.

lessons.question: When can a trigger execute?

lessons.title: FOR EACH ROW
lessons.content: FOR EACH ROW applies the trigger per row. Example: CREATE TRIGGER UpdateStock AFTER INSERT ON Orders FOR EACH ROW UPDATE Products SET Stock = Stock - 1;

lessons.question: What does FOR EACH ROW do?

lessons.title: NEW and OLD
lessons.content: Use NEW for inserted/updated rows, OLD for deleted/updated. Example: NEW.Quantity in an INSERT trigger.

lessons.question: What does NEW refer to in a trigger?

lessons.title: Creating Triggers
lessons.content: Use CREATE TRIGGER. Example: CREATE TRIGGER CheckPrice BEFORE INSERT ON Products FOR EACH ROW IF NEW.Price < 0 THEN SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'; END IF;

lessons.question: What creates a trigger?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Triggers can slow data operations. Keep trigger logic simple and avoid recursive triggers.

lessons.question: What can slow operations in triggers?

lessons.title: Dropping Triggers
lessons.content: Use DROP TRIGGER to remove. Example: DROP TRIGGER LogInsert;

lessons.question: How do you remove a trigger?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Triggers are used for logging changes, enforcing rules, or updating related tables automatically.
